Why Does Time Seem to Speed Up with Age?

Each year you live represents a smaller percentage of your life, and you perceive this time to pass by more quickly as compared to when you were younger. In addition, each year you age becomes less valuable because you have more of it. These two factors contribute to the perception that time goes faster as you age.

When you were 12 months old, 1 year represented 100% of your life. That time was important to you, because it represented 100% of your life. You perceived it as going by slowly because each month represented such a large portion of your life.

When you turn 50, one year is only 1/50th of your entire life - it doesn't hold as much perceptual "weight" as when you were younger, so time appears to fly by.

Plus, all the shit you do when you're younger are all "firsts". You value the first date, first kiss, first breakup etc. - all that happens only once, when you're younger, so the perceptual weight of that time is even greater.

I also think it's this, combined with the fact that most people tend to settle into pretty rigid daily routines as they get older. When you literally do the same things every day with very little variance, time will naturally seem to accelerate as your brain actually starts disregarding information because there is nothing new to process. That's why when you "zone out" time seems to fly as if you were asleep, because your brain was either busy processing some other bullshit that wasn't your perception of time or it was processing very little at all.

Your observance of time is very malleable, there's a reason we say it's relative. Want time to slow down? Do new things. Learn. Explore. Escape your routine, get out of your rut.

But remember, at the end of the day, the march of time is endless and unchanging, it is only your perception of it that changes.

Even if you go do something new... like, say... go to a foreign country, those things which are familiar to you will not get as much of your attention. You won't spend 5 minutes pondering the back seat of a cab and committing everything to memory or experience. After all, you've seen so many back seats. And the hotel room, you've seen a lot of those things before too. You don't need to investigate the coffee pot. Or the toilet. Or spend so much time playing with something because all of those pieces of imagination you've already covered time and again.

You're not filing away as many memories. You don't have as many snapshots of the time that passes. Think about it... I bet you can recall at least one childhood event with frightening clarity... the light, the sounds, the smells, the touch, the words, the emotions. Everything. Name one regular breakfast you had last year with that much clarity.

But if you were to go somewhere where everything is new. I mean everything. Let's say another planet with an alien species. Everything would be committed to some memory. You'd spend a looong time looking at their equivalent of a flower. Or their food. Or maybe their rocks. You would be committing so much new information that you'd essentially be as a child again, examining everything, playing with the possibilities, running those thought scenarios in your head... like the man in the toy car who go into an accident. You used to imagine that, and the crash, and the rescue, and the recovery. Those things were imagined and your brain works so much faster than real life. In maybe 15 minutes, that little man went through terror, injury, death and life, healing, and going back to normal. In real life, that would be months and months and months. You literally lived large span of an imaginary life in your head in the span of a few minutes.

So when you're older, you don't have to put as much into your memory.
